Cleveland’s offensive line currently ranks near the bottom of the league, while negative game scripts could limit rushing opportunities. The projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is neutral, and a fifth-round price near ADP 54 requires too many team and efficiency improvements.

summaries.card_summary: RJ Harvey is an attractive contingent back behind J.K. Dobbins, supported by Denver’s elite offensive line and scoring environment. His standalone price is fragile because touchdown regression, poor rushing efficiency, and a potential three-back committee could limit volume.
summaries.full_writeup:
Harvey’s appeal starts with his environment: Denver’s offensive line ranks first, and a strong offense can create valuable rushing and goal-line opportunities. If the backfield consolidates or J.K. Dobbins misses time, Harvey has the talent and situation to become a meaningful non-PPR starter. His prior receiving usage provides some additional utility, though his best fantasy path is through rushing volume and touchdowns rather than receptions.

The problem is that the current role is described as a primary handcuff, not a locked-in lead back. A committee would make his weekly workload difficult to trust, while the prior touchdown rate is expected to regress and his rushing efficiency has been poor. The projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is difficult. At an ADP around 7.08, the price assumes more dependable opportunity than the role currently establishes.

summaries.card_summary: Rachaad White is a cheap starter bet with a favorable projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule and potentially thin competition. In non-PPR, however, his receiving-based case is muted, and Washington’s bottom-ranked offensive line creates serious rushing-efficiency and touchdown concerns.
summaries.full_writeup:
White’s best argument is opportunity: he is listed as Washington’s projected starter, and the surrounding competition is described as thin. The projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is favorable, offering a modest boost if his workload is secure. His receiving skill can help keep him involved, but the larger non-PPR appeal would require meaningful rushing volume and enough scoring chances to overcome the team’s limitations.

Washington’s offensive line ranks last, creating a difficult foundation for efficient rushing and goal-line success. The team’s prior running-back target share was low, so there is not strong evidence that a reception-heavy role will carry his value in this format. White is better suited as a low-cost depth gamble than a player to select aggressively; his RB39 market range appropriately reflects the uncertainty.

summaries.card_summary: Rashee Rice still has legitimate WR1 upside when active, with proven target earning, red-zone opportunity, and a strong offensive line. The risk is too large for his WR13 cost because suspension, knee recovery, availability, off-field issues, and changing team priorities could erase the value.
summaries.full_writeup:
Rice’s football ceiling remains compelling. When active, he has demonstrated the ability to earn substantial usage, and his short-area volume can translate into yardage, touchdowns, and occasional big plays even without PPR scoring. Kansas City’s strong offensive line supports the passing environment, while his red-zone role and status as a physically imposing receiver preserve a path to high-end production during available games.

Availability is the central problem, not a minor deduction. Dated reporting has included knee, suspension, and off-field uncertainty, and those issues make his weekly and season-long workload difficult to price. A changing Kansas City offense and meaningful receiver competition add further volatility, while the projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is difficult. At a WR13 or early-round price, the discount is insufficient unless his health and availability clear decisively.

summaries.card_summary: Shaheed is an appealing late non-PPR flier because his explosive playmaking could earn Seattle’s No. 2 receiver role and produce spike weeks through yardage and touchdowns. The case remains usage-dependent with Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp, and Tory Horton competing for targets.
summaries.full_writeup:
Shaheed offers legitimate late-round upside if Seattle gives him a larger role after a full offseason with the team. His big-play skill set can matter in non-PPR through receiving yardage, long touchdowns, and designed touches, while prior-season involvement provides at least some evidence of a usable offensive role. A neutral projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule neither materially boosts nor hurts the case, and his current WR54 market range leaves room for profit if he wins meaningful snaps.

Shaheed’s value is less attractive if his production depends mainly on occasional receptions rather than consistent yardage, touchdowns, or rushing/design work, so he fits best as a cheap upside reserve rather than a player to force at a premium.

summaries.card_summary: Bateman is a deep non-PPR dart whose favorable projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule offers a small tiebreaker, but his path requires a major role rebound. The limited prior-season usage, weak offensive line, and thin support make him highly price-sensitive.
summaries.full_writeup:
Bateman has a plausible rebound path if Baltimore expands his route volume and he converts his opportunities into meaningful yardage and touchdowns. His current WR74 non-PPR market range reflects a low acquisition cost, and the projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is favorable enough to provide modest support. In a non-PPR league, a breakout would need to come from increased downfield involvement and scoring rather than simply accumulating catches.

The baseline is fragile: Bateman had a very limited prior-season target role, and the team’s current offensive line ranks in the weak tier, which can undermine developing passing production. The lone positive sleeper view is also less persuasive than a broadly established role, so there is little margin for paying above a late-round flier price. He is a speculative bench option, not a dependable weekly starter.

summaries.card_summary: Stevenson is a reasonable non-PPR value around his RB27 market range, with projected starting status and a path to substantial early-down and goal-line work. His outlook depends on maintaining the role while Henderson’s availability and trust improve, and the difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is a minor negative.
summaries.full_writeup:
Stevenson has inexpensive access to a potentially substantial backfield role, particularly if the larger playoff snap share carries into the regular season. The projected starter designation supports his floor, and his strongest non-PPR appeal comes from carries, goal-line opportunities, and touchdown access rather than receiving volume. A middle-tier offensive line is adequate for a usable workload, making him a sensible target near the current RB27 market range if the backfield remains unsettled.

Henderson can reclaim meaningful work once healthy and trusted in pass protection, leaving Stevenson vulnerable to a committee or reduced passing-down role. His prior-season receiving involvement was limited, which matters less in non-PPR but still reduces his paths to production if rushing volume disappoints. The difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule adds some resistance, so the price should reflect role uncertainty rather than assume a locked-in workhorse.

summaries.card_summary: Dowdle is a viable late non-PPR target because Pittsburgh’s unsettled backfield gives him a path to lead-back carries and touchdowns at a modest price. Jaylen Warren’s competing role and a difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule make a full workload far from certain.
summaries.full_writeup:
Dowdle’s appeal is straightforward: an unsettled Pittsburgh backfield could elevate him into the lead role without a significant draft-day cost. The projected starter designation and middle-tier offensive line support a reasonable workload case, while a lead-back role would create the rushing volume and touchdown opportunities that matter most in non-PPR. His current RB31 market range is compatible with taking a calculated chance on expanded carries rather than paying for certainty.

Warren can retain meaningful work, preventing Dowdle from becoming a reliable every-down option. Prior-season target involvement offers some receiving support, but those catches are less valuable in this format and should not carry the evaluation. The difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is another modest obstacle, so Dowdle needs the backfield opportunity to translate into consistent rushing volume rather than merely sharing a murky rotation.

summaries.card_summary: Odunze is a strong non-PPR target around the sixth round because his encouraging early 2025 stretch, Moore’s departure, and a strong offensive line create a clearer path to yardage and touchdowns. The valuation assumes he stays healthy and wins enough work from Luther Burden and Colston Loveland.
summaries.full_writeup:
Odunze has the best profile here for a meaningful non-PPR breakout. His strong pre-injury start in 2025 showed encouraging involvement, and Moore’s departure creates a cleaner route to lead-receiver opportunity. A strong offensive line should help sustain the passing game, while Odunze’s upside can come from receiving yardage and touchdowns rather than requiring heavy reception totals. His current WR26 consensus range and sixth-round pricing are reasonable for a player with a plausible top-12 ceiling.

The breakout is not automatic. Burden and Loveland still compete for targets, and the case depends on Odunze carrying his pre-injury form across a full season. A neutral projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule provides no special advantage, so the investment is primarily about talent and role growth. He is attractive at the stated range, but the price becomes less appealing if drafters pay for the ceiling as though target competition has disappeared.

summaries.card_summary: Flournoy is a deep-league flier whose stable third-receiver role could become valuable in a strong passing offense if a starter misses time. His normal workload is limited behind two stars, and the case is less compelling in non-PPR unless targets or touchdowns rise.
summaries.full_writeup:
Flournoy offers cheap contingency value in a strong passing offense, with a defined third-receiver role and a path to immediate relevance if either starting wideout misses time. That role could produce useful yardage and touchdown opportunities, particularly at a final-round price. His current non-PPR market standing around WR70 reflects a bench stash rather than a weekly starter, which is appropriate for the profile.

The central problem is limited standalone volume: his prior-season usage was modest, and he remains behind two high-volume receivers. A difficult projected 2026 regular-season schedule adds a minor concern, while his upside depends heavily on an injury opening or a meaningful expansion in route and red-zone work. He is a reasonable late flier, not a player to chase based mainly on reception-driven sleeper logic.

summaries.card_summary: LaPorta retains elite-offense and touchdown upside, but TE6 pricing leaves less room for his crowded target tree and injury risk. In non-PPR, he is attractive only if the price falls below the premium tier.
summaries.full_writeup:
LaPorta remains a talented scoring option in an elite offense, and his touchdown ceiling can still separate him from lower-tier tight ends. The current non-PPR consensus places him firmly in the premium TE tier, reflecting the possibility that efficient red-zone usage overcomes a crowded passing game. A neutral projected 2026 regular-season tight-end schedule neither materially helps nor hurts the case.

The concern is that premium cost assumes reliable volume from a player competing for targets in a busy offense. His multi-year injury history adds volatility, and a dated August 25 report said he had only recently returned to practice from a hip injury, with Week 1 status still murky despite the positive progression. At a reduced price he is appealing; at TE6 cost, the downside is substantial.

summaries.card_summary: Tucker is a strong-offensive-line contingency back with spike-week potential, but he needs an injury or major role change to matter. In a 10-team non-PPR league, he belongs only in the final rounds.
summaries.full_writeup:
Tucker has worthwhile late-round contingency appeal because the current offensive line ranks in the league’s strong tier, giving any expanded rushing role a favorable foundation. He has demonstrated the ability to produce a spike week, and a backfield injury could quickly turn him into a useful source of carries and touchdowns. His RB62 market context fits a speculative bench stash.

His standalone case is extremely thin: prior-season involvement was minimal, particularly as a receiver, and the expectation is that he needs an injury ahead of him. That limitation matters less in non-PPR than in reception-heavy formats, but it still leaves him without a dependable weekly workload. The projected 2026 regular-season running-back schedule is difficult, making him strictly a final-round contingency play.

summaries.card_summary: Diggs offers inexpensive WR2 potential if his Washington 1B role produces meaningful yardage and touchdowns, but age, Terry McLaurin, a weak offensive line, and a difficult projected schedule create real downside. His non-PPR value depends more on efficiency and scoring than receptions.
summaries.full_writeup:
Diggs brings a credible rebound case as Washington’s potential 1B receiver, with prior-season involvement showing he can still command meaningful work. If he converts that role into strong yardage and touchdown production, his rounds 9-10 price could yield WR2 value even without reception scoring. The non-PPR setup makes his efficiency and scoring potential more important than simply accumulating catches.

The risks are significant. McLaurin remains a major competing target, Diggs is aging, and the team’s offensive line ranks last in the league’s current preseason evaluation, which could suppress passing efficiency. The projected 2026 regular-season wide-receiver schedule is also difficult. His current non-PPR WR50 market range is defensible as a discount, but the 1B role and offensive environment must hold for the upside to materialize.

summaries.card_summary: Hockenson is an appealing late rebound target if improved quarterback play restores his volume and red-zone usefulness. His TE24 price is reasonable, but declining usage, age, and the health/transition assumptions make him less attractive at a premium.
summaries.full_writeup:
Hockenson has a plausible bounce-back path through improved quarterback play, better health, and a potentially favorable passing environment. His underlying ability to get open and convert opportunities supports a return to useful yardage and touchdown production, while the projected 2026 regular-season tight-end schedule is favorable. At roughly TE24 market cost, the rebound is inexpensive enough to pursue in a 10-team league if the top tiers are gone.

The downside is that his target share and efficiency have declined across multiple seasons, so a single quarterback change may not fully restore prior production. Age and recovery concerns remain meaningful assumptions, even with reports framing him as healthy entering the season. In non-PPR, he needs substantive yardage or touchdown improvement rather than merely a modest reception increase, making him a value pick rather than a safe weekly starter.

summaries.card_summary: Tank Bigsby is a low-cost handcuff with meaningful RB2 contingency value if Saquon Barkley misses time. His standalone outlook is limited, so the case depends on roster construction, price, and Barkley’s health.
summaries.full_writeup:
Bigsby’s clearest value is contingency-based: he is listed as Barkley’s primary handcuff and could step into an RB2 role if the starter is unavailable. A top-tier offensive line and favorable projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule would support efficient rushing production in that scenario. At a late-round cost, he can be a sensible insurance pick in a non-PPR auction league, where a rushing workload and touchdowns matter more than receiving volume.

The problem is that he has little standalone value while Barkley is healthy. His prior-season receiving involvement was extremely limited, reinforcing that he needs rushing volume to matter. The handcuff role, team environment, and price could change before the season, and a favorable schedule is only a modest tiebreaker. He is more useful to a Barkley roster or a deep bench than as an independent weekly target.

summaries.card_summary: Tank Dell is a speculative late-round receiver whose appeal comes from upside rather than a secure role. In non-PPR, weak offensive-line conditions and uncertain touchdown access make him difficult to prioritize unless the price falls well beyond his current market range.
summaries.full_writeup:
Dell has enough perceived upside to merit consideration as a late dart throw, particularly if he earns a meaningful role in a receiving corps with established target volume. His current non-PPR ranking places him around the back-end WR7 range, leaving room for profit if he becomes a consistent downfield or scoring threat. The neutral projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule neither materially strengthens nor weakens the case.

The floor is fragile. A weak offensive line can restrict route development and reduce big-play opportunities, while the available information does not establish dependable weekly usage or touchdown volume. Reception-driven sleeper appeal is less powerful in non-PPR than in formats rewarding catches, so he should not be drafted aggressively on speculative target accumulation alone. Treat him as a low-cost upside reserve rather than a planned starter.

summaries.card_summary: Tee Higgins is a strong non-PPR target whose discounted WR16 market standing reflects real upside in a concentrated Cincinnati offense. His ceiling still depends on health, Ja’Marr Chase’s dominance, and the offensive line remaining functional.
summaries.full_writeup:
Higgins offers the profile of a dependable yardage-and-touchdown contributor in a capable offense. Cincinnati’s passing game has concentrated its wide-receiver opportunities, and Higgins has already demonstrated substantial involvement rather than relying solely on occasional splash plays. The projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is favorable, providing a modest boost, while his current non-PPR market range leaves room for a strong return if he remains healthy and retains a prominent role opposite Chase.

Chase limits Higgins’ path to becoming the unquestioned focal point, so his target ceiling is naturally capped. Higgins also carries health sensitivity, and Cincinnati’s middle-tier offensive line does not remove all concerns about consistency. The favorable schedule should not justify an inflated auction price, particularly if the market pushes him above his WR16-type valuation. He is attractive at a discount, but less compelling when priced as a guaranteed top-tier receiver.

summaries.card_summary: Terry McLaurin remains an appealing non-PPR target at a discount because he can regain substantial yardage and touchdown production as Washington’s expected WR1. Stefon Diggs’ arrival, a weak offensive line, and a difficult projected schedule make full-price drafting risky.
summaries.full_writeup:
McLaurin’s favorable case rests on lead-receiver opportunity and a potentially healthier Washington passing attack. Multiple evaluations point to more targets and a return toward his established 1,000-yard-level profile if healthy, while the team’s prior receiving usage was concentrated among its top options. A dated August 22 report had him expected to play against Detroit, which is encouraging but does not eliminate the broader health assumption. At a one-round discount, his big-play ability and touchdown potential remain attractive in non-PPR.

The downside is more substantial than his WR24 market rank implies. Diggs creates legitimate competition for valuable targets, and Washington’s weak offensive line plus difficult projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule could depress efficiency. A scramble-heavy offense may also produce uneven passing volume. McLaurin can outperform his price if he stays healthy and remains the clear first option, but paying around a low-end WR2 valuation leaves limited margin for those role and environment concerns.

summaries.card_summary: Tetairoa McMillan has a strong Year 2 breakout case after meaningful rookie involvement and limited added competition. His WR18 price is aggressive in non-PPR, where the outcome depends heavily on Bryce Young’s improvement, touchdown growth, and Carolina’s weak offensive environment.
summaries.full_writeup:
McMillan’s upside comes from a substantial rookie role that can expand in his second season. His target share was characterized as a strong foundation, and limited new competition gives him a plausible path to lead Carolina in receiving production. If Bryce Young continues improving, McMillan could combine volume, yardage, and touchdowns into a difference-making non-PPR season. That growth potential explains why he remains valued near the top 20 at receiver.

The opposing case is that the offense may not generate enough efficient drives to support that price. Carolina’s weak offensive line and difficult projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule add pressure to an already quarterback-dependent breakout, while Jalen Coker could reduce McMillan’s market share. Touchdown growth is also required to fully justify an aggressive valuation. He is a legitimate upside target, but in a 10-team non-PPR auction, the WR18 cost leaves less room for disappointment than a later breakout price would.

summaries.card_summary: Pollard is a reasonable RB3-price target because a dominant role and limited competition provide volume-based RB1 upside if Tennessee improves. The weak offensive line and his low 2025 efficiency make him price-sensitive in non-PPR.
summaries.full_writeup:
Pollard’s strongest case is workload: he is projected to start, faces limited competition, and could command enough rushing volume to matter even without heavy receiving production. That path becomes much more attractive at an RB3 price, particularly if Tennessee’s offense improves and creates more touchdown opportunities. The neutral projected 2026 regular-season schedule neither materially helps nor hurts the outlook.

The concern is that similar workload produced only an RB30 points-per-game finish in 2025, a meaningful warning for non-PPR scoring. Tennessee’s offensive line currently ranks 29th, which threatens rushing efficiency and scoring chances, while his modest prior receiving usage offers little reception-based cushion. He is a worthwhile value bet, but not a player to pay an RB2 price for.

summaries.card_summary: Etienne is a solid non-PPR value around his RB18 market cost, with a clear lead role and established workload giving him upper-RB2 potential. The price already reflects much of the opportunity, and his upside depends on retaining that role while the backfield changes.
summaries.full_writeup:
Etienne has the clearest workload case among these backs: he is projected to start and should benefit from a lead role while Kamara recovers. His prior usage demonstrates a meaningful offensive role, with enough rushing volume and receiving involvement to support upper-RB2 production even though receptions matter less in this format. A middle-tier offensive line and neutral projected 2026 regular-season schedule provide a stable, if unspectacular, environment.

The main issue is cost. Around RB18 or a fourth-round pick, Etienne is being drafted as a reliable contributor rather than a true late bargain. His outlook is also tied to the backfield situation; the value can deteriorate if his expected lead role shrinks. The prior-season team target share was modest, so his non-PPR ceiling should come primarily from rushing volume and touchdowns rather than receptions.

summaries.card_summary: Hunter is only a speculative late-round flyer in this non-PPR league: a favorable projected 2026 regular-season schedule and team target volume offer upside, but his current WR73 market rank reflects substantial role uncertainty. Do not pay for a half-PPR sleeper case built mainly on receptions.
summaries.full_writeup:
Hunter’s favorable elements are opportunity and matchup environment. His team’s 2025 receivers commanded a strong share of available targets, and the projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is favorable. If his role expands substantially, that team context could support useful yardage and touchdown production, especially at a minimal price.

The case is too uncertain for an aggressive bid. His 2025 target volume was limited, the offensive line ranks 30th, and the current non-PPR market places him at WR73 with a very wide range of outcomes. The sleeper argument comes from a single half-PPR assessment, so it should be heavily discounted here: without clear downfield production or red-zone usage, receptions alone will not make him valuable.

summaries.card_summary: Kelce is an avoid at a strong-ADP price near 90 because declining touchdown output and added target competition undermine his former elite advantage. His quarterback connection, strong line, and favorable projected schedule keep him viable, but the non-PPR margin for error is thin.
summaries.full_writeup:
Kelce still has a credible floor through quarterback chemistry, a strong offensive line, and a team tight-end group that accounted for a substantial share of targets in 2025. He led Kansas City in receiving last season, and the projected 2026 regular-season TE schedule is favorable. Those factors make him a plausible starter if he falls well below his usual name-driven cost.

The problem is that his historical edge is eroding. Touchdown output has declined, and broader competition for targets makes it harder to project dominant volume. In non-PPR scoring, his reception totals provide less separation, so he needs strong yardage or touchdown production to justify a pick near 90. With the current market ranking around TE11, he is better treated as a discounted veteran than a premium tight end.

summaries.card_summary: Tucker is an appealing late-round non-PPR value if his emerging WR1 role holds, with cheap access to increased routes, designed touches, and touchdown upside. The weak Raiders passing environment, Brock Bowers’ target presence, and a difficult projected schedule cap confidence.
summaries.full_writeup:
Tucker’s favorable case rests on role rather than reception scoring. He is described as Las Vegas’ lead receiver, already has heavy playing-time expectations, and could gain designed touches and more downfield opportunities at a late-round cost. His prior target volume was meaningful for a developing receiver, while the offensive line ranks in the middle tier rather than the league’s weakest group. Multiple market evaluations place him well ahead of his inexpensive draft cost.

The offense remains the central obstacle. Bowers is still positioned as the passing game’s focal point, and quarterback and coordinator changes limit certainty about whether Tucker’s role becomes productive yardage and touchdowns. The projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is difficult, further reducing his weekly reliability. In non-PPR, he needs actual receiving production—not merely a high catch total—to beat his price, so he is a worthwhile cheap flier rather than a player to reach for.

summaries.card_summary: Tre' Harris is a speculative late-round Chargers receiver whose path depends on earning a larger role after limited 2025 involvement. The upside is appealing at a cheap price, but his role, health, and difficult projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule remain concerns in non-PPR.
summaries.full_writeup:
Harris offers inexpensive upside if he converts an uneven rookie season into a meaningful Chargers role. The current market places him around the WR66 range, while some evaluations view him as a late-round value, making him a reasonable bench swing in a 10-team non-PPR auction. A strong offensive line could support the passing game, and the franchise’s 2025 receivers held a substantial target share, though personnel and scheme may change.

The central problem is that Harris had only limited 2025 usage, so the larger-role thesis is almost entirely forward-looking. In non-PPR, he needs dependable yardage and touchdown involvement rather than merely accumulating catches, and there is no established workload here. His difficult projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is a modest additional negative. Keep the price low and treat him as a role-dependent flier, not a roster cornerstone.

summaries.card_summary: TreVeyon Henderson has three-down upside and strong per-snap production, but his value is highly sensitive to the Rhamondre Stevenson split. The ankle issue is currently described as minor, yet his RB22-level price is risky if Stevenson remains the postseason workload leader.
summaries.full_writeup:
Henderson’s favorable case rests on explosive efficiency and a proven three-down ceiling, giving him legitimate non-PPR upside through rushing volume, yardage, and touchdowns. His 2025 receiving involvement also provides some utility, while the Patriots’ backfield generated meaningful target work overall. The market consensus places him near RB26, which is more reasonable than treating him as an unquestioned early-backfield leader.

The major disagreement is role: one view sees Henderson priced as the leader, while another emphasizes Stevenson’s control of the postseason workload. Henderson was also not practicing on August 25 because of an ankle injury, though the issue was not expected to be serious; that status needs updating before paying full price. A middle-tier offensive line and difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule add modest concerns. He is attractive only if the auction discount reflects genuine committee risk.

summaries.card_summary: Trevor Lawrence is an appealing midrange QB option after a strong second half and useful rushing production in Liam Coen’s offense. Touchdown regression and a weak offensive line keep him from being a clear bargain at his QB10 market standing.
summaries.full_writeup:
Lawrence’s case is built on a QB1-level 2025 finish, a strong late-season run, rushing contributions, and continuity in Liam Coen’s offense. Those rushing points matter in standard scoring because they do not depend on receptions, and the projected 2026 regular-season QB schedule is favorable as a modest tiebreaker. His current QB10 consensus range supports viewing him as a viable starter rather than a desperation option.

The clearest risk is regression in rushing touchdowns, which helped elevate his prior finish and may not repeat. More importantly, Jacksonville’s current offensive line ranks in the weak tier, creating pressure on both passing efficiency and scoring opportunities. The favorable schedule cannot fully offset that structural concern. Lawrence is a solid target at a reasonable quarterback price, but he should not be valued as though last season’s rushing-touchdown rate is guaranteed.

summaries.card_summary: Tucker Kraft offers top-five tight-end upside if his ACL recovery reaches full strength, and his August 26 return to 11-on-11 work was encouraging. However, a possible early snap limitation and weak offensive line make his TE5 price dependent on immediate health and usage.
summaries.full_writeup:
Kraft’s pre-injury scoring pace and central role in Green Bay create a strong non-PPR ceiling through touchdowns, yardage, and efficient red-zone usage. The Packers’ tight ends accounted for a meaningful share of team targets in 2025, and vacated opportunities could support Kraft if his role remains intact. His return to 11-on-11 drills on August 26, after earlier team work, suggested he remained on track for Week 1, supporting the discounted upside case.

The risk is not talent but recovery. Kraft is returning from an ACL tear, and one competing view considers his timetable too uncertain to justify a TE5 price; even if active, an early snap cap could suppress production. The weak offensive line and difficult projected 2026 regular-season TE schedule are secondary concerns. In a standard league, pay for the possibility of a full role rather than assuming it, and avoid forcing the valuation if his cost approaches established healthy tight ends.

summaries.card_summary: Tyjae Spears is a cheap handcuff with some standalone appeal, but his non-PPR value is heavily dependent on Tony Pollard missing time. A weak offensive line and limited touchdown certainty make him more of a late bench stash than a weekly starter.
summaries.full_writeup:
Spears is a sensible late-round contingency play behind Tony Pollard, with a path to meaningful rushing volume if the depth chart changes. His 2025 target involvement gives him some additional utility, but the non-PPR format places greater emphasis on whether he receives carries, goal-line work, and reliable yardage. He is being valued around the RB50 range, making the handcuff upside relatively inexpensive in a 10-team auction.

The problem is that his useful role may remain contingent rather than secure. The Titans’ offensive line ranks in the weak tier, which could limit rushing efficiency, while a neutral projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule offers no meaningful boost. A backfield target share from 2025 is only background context because personnel and scheme may change. Spears is worth a minimal bid if roster space allows, but the case is not strong enough to prioritize him over backs with clearer weekly workloads.

summaries.card_summary: Allgeier is a cheap early-season volume and goal-line bet who can produce flex weeks while Jeremiyah Love recovers, with some short-yardage value afterward. The ceiling is modest because Arizona’s scoring environment, difficult projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule, and Love’s eventual workload could limit him.
summaries.full_writeup:
Allgeier’s strongest case is immediate opportunity: he is positioned for early carries and goal-line work while Jeremiyah Love recovers. That role can generate useful non-PPR production through rushing volume and touchdowns, and short-yardage usage could preserve occasional flex relevance even after Love returns. His low acquisition cost makes the bet easier to justify, particularly if the backfield hierarchy remains unsettled into the season.

The concern is that the offense may not create enough scoring chances to support dependable touchdown production. Arizona’s offensive line ranks in the middle tier, while the projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is difficult, making efficiency and weekly reliability less appealing. Allgeier’s limited prior receiving involvement offers little non-PPR help, and Love reclaiming most of the backfield would leave Allgeier dependent on goal-line work or an injury ahead of him.

summaries.card_summary: Shough is an inexpensive quarterback sleeper whose late-2025 scoring pace, rushing ability near the goal line, and improving weapons create legitimate breakout appeal. The case depends on a small NFL sample, touchdown growth, and receiving health, so he fits best as a late-round QB2.
summaries.full_writeup:
Shough’s upside comes from multiple paths to fantasy points: his strong late-2025 starting pace, added offensive weapons, and potential goal-line rushing can support useful non-PPR quarterback production. A healthier receiving group, particularly if Jordyn Tyson returns effectively, could raise his passing ceiling, while his current QB20-area market cost leaves room for profit. The offensive line ranks in the middle tier, and the projected 2026 regular-season QB schedule is neutral rather than a major obstacle.

The breakout still relies heavily on a limited NFL sample and projected touchdown improvement. If the early receiving group is less healthy or effective than expected, Shough’s passing efficiency and scoring opportunities could remain ordinary. His market appeal weakens if the price rises toward a weekly starter cost, because the neutral schedule and middle-tier line do not independently create a strong floor.

summaries.card_summary: Warren is a strong non-PPR tight end target thanks to substantial prior volume, a strong offensive line, and a plausible second-year touchdown and efficiency jump. He is worth paying near the current market, but not an excessive premium because his rookie production lacked elite efficiency and touchdown access, and his groin issue remains a live short-term concern.
summaries.full_writeup:
Warren already demonstrated a substantial role with 112 targets in 2025, and the team’s tight ends collectively held a meaningful 26.3% target share. That workload gives him a strong non-PPR foundation, while a second-year leap in efficiency or touchdowns could separate him from the middle tier. A top-four consensus market standing reflects his upside, and the team’s fourth-ranked offensive line should support sustained offensive functionality. Vacated targets could further reinforce his opportunity if the new distribution favors him.

The central risk is price: a premium tight-end cost requires more than volume and assumes better efficiency and scoring than he showed as a rookie. The projected 2026 regular-season TE schedule is neutral, so it offers no meaningful discount. Warren was not practicing as of August 26 while recovering from a groin injury; Week 1 was not considered in danger at that time, but a setback would alter the outlook. Paying near the top of the position leaves less margin for that uncertainty.

summaries.card_summary: Tracy is a useful late bench target with receiving involvement and RB2 upside if Cam Skattebo misses time. His standalone non-PPR ceiling is limited while Skattebo is healthy, and a weak offensive line adds efficiency risk despite a favorable projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule.
summaries.full_writeup:
Tracy’s appeal is role-based but meaningful: his prior receiving involvement gives him a path to extra touches, while an expanded rushing role could produce RB2 value if Cam Skattebo is unavailable. That versatility matters in non-PPR because receiving work helps only when it creates yardage or additional touches, but Tracy’s ability to contribute in both phases still improves his contingency value. The projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule is favorable, providing a modest boost if he becomes the lead option.

A healthy Skattebo reportedly controls the early-down workload, leaving Tracy with a capped weekly touch floor and limited standalone ceiling. His team’s offensive line ranks near the bottom of the league, which could depress rushing efficiency and touchdown chances. The backfield’s prior target share was meaningful but not overwhelming, so Tracy should not be drafted as though receiving usage alone guarantees production. His value is strongest at a late price that pays for insurance rather than a locked-in starting role.

summaries.card_summary: Robinson’s established volume and continuity in the offense make him a reasonable late target, but non-PPR managers should discount the reception-driven floor. He needs strong yardage or touchdown conversion to beat his price, with Carnell Tate, Calvin Ridley, a weak offensive line, and uncertain passing volume creating real downside.
summaries.full_writeup:
Robinson brings proven opportunity, with 140 targets in 2025 and continuity in Brian Daboll’s system. That history supports a significant role, and the team’s wide receivers accounted for 56.0% of targets last season, suggesting the offense can continue leaning on its pass catchers. At a late-round cost, his route familiarity and short-area usage can still produce value if it translates into dependable yardage and occasional touchdowns. The projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is neutral, so it neither materially boosts nor undermines the outlook.

The problem in this non-PPR format is that Robinson’s appeal is heavily tied to reception volume rather than demonstrated scoring or explosive yardage. Carnell Tate and Calvin Ridley create meaningful competition, while the offensive line ranks 29th and could depress the team’s passing efficiency and total scoring. Tennessee’s overall passing ceiling is also uncertain. Robinson is defensible around a WR4/late-round price, but a higher cost would require assuming that his volume converts into more yardage and touchdowns than his profile has established.

summaries.card_summary: Late-round contingency value: Woody Marks could become an RB2 if David Montgomery misses time, with third-down work giving him a path to usefulness even in non-PPR. His value depends heavily on Montgomery’s health, while the weak offensive line and Montgomery’s projected early-down and goal-line control limit the standalone case.
summaries.full_writeup:
Marks offers a sensible late-round contingency bet. He is reportedly earning third-down and receiving work, and the backfield may be closer to a split than his current price suggests. If Montgomery misses time, Marks could inherit enough rushing volume to matter as an RB2, with a favorable projected 2026 regular-season running-back schedule providing a modest boost. His receiving role is less valuable in non-PPR than in reception-scoring formats, but it still supports playing-time stability.

The primary problem is that Marks needs a change in circumstances to become a reliable starter. Montgomery is still projected to handle early downs and goal-line work, the most valuable non-PPR opportunities, and the offensive line ranks in the league’s weak tier. Treat Marks as a late target around his inexpensive market cost, not as a player with secure weekly volume.

summaries.card_summary: Xavier Worthy is a reasonable post-hype late value if his price reflects a volatile role and his big-play ability converts into yardage and touchdowns. The strong offensive line helps, but a difficult projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule and only modest prior-season involvement make him more of a calculated flier in non-PPR.
summaries.full_writeup:
Worthy’s appeal comes from talent and rebound potential after a disappointing market reaction. His speed can create explosive yardage and touchdown plays, which matters more in non-PPR than reception accumulation, and the team’s offensive line ranks in the strong tier. A late discount gives him room to outperform expectations if his role expands and the passing attack creates more consistent downfield opportunities.

The player-specific case remains relatively thin, and Worthy’s prior-season role was not yet that of a dependable volume receiver. That creates substantial weekly volatility, especially when receptions provide no scoring floor. The projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is difficult, so he should be drafted as a low-cost upside swing rather than a player whose market price assumes a full breakout.

summaries.card_summary: Zach Charbonnet has touchdown and committee appeal if he returns healthy, with a favorable projected 2026 regular-season RB schedule supporting the stash. His ACL recovery could keep him out into October, making role, availability, and price the central concerns.
summaries.full_writeup:
Charbonnet could regain a committee role with access to valuable rushing and goal-line work once healthy. Those touches offer a stronger non-PPR foundation than a receiving-dependent profile, and the projected 2026 regular-season running-back schedule is favorable. A mid-tier offensive line is less concerning than an outright liability, while his current RB47 market range leaves room for value if he returns near form and immediately reclaims meaningful work.

The timeline is the major obstacle. ACL rehabilitation may extend into October, so Charbonnet could provide little early-season value and may face an uncertain workload when he returns. His previous receiving involvement was limited, reducing the fallback value if rushing opportunities are scarce. He is better suited to a patient bench spot at a cheap price than to a pick that requires immediate production.

summaries.card_summary: Zachariah Branch is an intriguing deep dynasty stash whose playmaking could earn designed touches, but he is not an appealing 2026 non-PPR redraft target at his current level of role uncertainty. The strong offensive line helps the offense, yet his WR82 market context reflects a limited immediate path.
summaries.full_writeup:
Branch’s upside rests on explosive ability and the possibility that the offense manufactures touches for him. A strong offensive line and a generally healthy team passing environment could help those opportunities become meaningful, while designed rushing or scoring plays would be particularly useful in non-PPR. He makes more sense as a developmental asset than as a player who must immediately carry a fantasy lineup.

The concern is the absence of an established 2026 redraft role. The positive dynasty framing does not establish dependable season-long volume, and reception-driven production would offer little benefit without enough yardage or touchdowns. His WR82 consensus range and low projected 2026 standing point toward a waiver-wire or very late-draft profile in a 10-team league, unless his price is essentially free.

summaries.card_summary: Zay Flowers is a strong non-PPR target near his WR14 market range because his established volume, efficiency, and potential touchdown growth can support a true WR1 season. Baltimore’s passing volume remains a concern, and his dated August 26 ankle-related practice absences require monitoring rather than being treated as a current injury conclusion.
summaries.full_writeup:
Flowers has the clearest premium case of this group. He has already demonstrated substantial involvement, brings elite route efficiency, and could gain fantasy value through touchdown improvement rather than relying solely on receptions. Limited competition and strong team commitment support a prominent role, while the projected 2026 regular-season WR schedule is favorable. In non-PPR, his route-winning ability and scoring upside are especially important because they can convert volume into yardage and touchdowns.

The offense may still produce uneven passing volume, which can create inconsistency even for a dominant receiver. The offensive line currently ranks in the weak tier, another potential drag on passing efficiency. More immediately, Flowers missed practice on August 24 and August 26 after reportedly tweaking an ankle; that dated news should be monitored for updates before paying a premium price.
